CASH BOX JULY 31 ,1993 8 TALENT REVIEW David Benoit By Brad Pressman k m THE GREEK THEATRE, LOS ANGELES, CA—If you like loud guitars, electrifying lights and 50,000 megawatts of power.. .go see Def Leppard! On the other hand, if you enjoy a wonderful evening under the stars listening to some great Contemporary Jazz, the Greek Theatre was the place to be last week. David Benoit was the man of the hour, playing some of the best instrumental melodies that have delighted his fans for years. "Letter To Evan," the title track from his newest CD, began the set after Kenny Rankin and Strunz & Farah began the evening. From there, Benoit took the crowd on a musical journey that featured a 12-piece orchestra and a couple of special guests: sax pro Eric Marienthal, who plays on most of Benoit's albums, and Russ Freeman, the lead guitarist for the Rippingtons. Benoit and Freeman, in fact, announced that they will release an album together sometime soon. They treated the audience to a preview of what that effort might be like. The crowd really got into things after hearing such Benoit signa- tures as "Linus & Lucy" and "Kei's Song." By the end of the evening, there were 22 players on stage belting out these incredible songs most of us know from Benoit's studio work. If you closed your eyes for a minute, you'd have sworn you were at the Hol- lywood Bowl listening to the L.A. Philharmonic. But then you opened them and saw individuals who, without a doubt, are at the top of their profession in Contemporary Jazz. All in all, it was just a beautiful evening of great music, great weather and a great setting. Paul Westerberg/School Of Fish By Troy ]. Augusto THE WHISKY, WEST HOLLYWOOD, CA—Anticipation was high, very high actually, for this, Paul Westerberg's first post-Re- placements Los Angeles appearance. And to say that Paul's fans got their money's worth would be a severe understatement. Ninety minutes was given to tracks from his amazing new Sire album, 14 Songs, as well as faves and more obscure cuts from most of the 'Mats (the Replacements' nickname) releases. The (over) packed house was treated to the best of Paul's solo work, including show-opener "Waiting For Somebody" (from the Singles soundtrack), thepunk-y "Down Love," the subtly infectious "Dice Behind Your Shades" and the Rolling Stones-y "Knockin' On Mine." Kept honest by a most rambunctious backing band, Wester- berg appeared both confident and comfortable as song after song was greeted with increasingly loud applause. Surprising to many was the large number of Replacements' songs that Westerberg offered. Silly "Waitress In The Sky," "Left Of The Dial," both from the fine Tim album, "I Will Dare" and crowd- pleaser "I'll Be You" were the best of the 'Mats lot. Also included in the sweaty set was a goof cover of the Monkees' "Daydream Believer" and "Another Planet," originally recorded by obscure British band The Lonely Ones. After the show, the first of two at the Whisky, Westerberg greeted friends and well-wishers in the cramped dressing room area and seemed exhausted but pleased with the show, a preview of sorts for an expected L.A. theater appearance later this summer. L. A.'s own School Of Fisn opened the evening with an enjoyable set of stripped-down, alt-rock tunes from its two Capitol albums. A fine companion act for Westerberg, "Complicated," "Half A Believer," both from the band's new Human Cannonball release and "3 Straight Days," a semi-hit from the quartet's debut, were high- lights. Blue Note Records celebrates the U.S. performance debut by Cuban pianist and label signee, Gonzalo Rubalcaba. The sold-out concert at Lincoln Center drew a cast of numerous musicians and well-wishers. Pictured (l-r) are: Manhattan Records artist Everette Harp; bassist Charlie Haden; Somethin’ Else president Hitoshi Namekata; Rubalcaba’s manager Jose Forteza; Rubalcaba; Blue Note producer Michael Cuscuna; Capitol/Blue Note artist Rachelle Ferrell; bassist Reynaldo Melian; Blue Note artist Jack DeJohnette; and Blue Note president Bruce Lundvall.

DARRYL & (Epic 53559) DON ELLIS "10 Minutes Till blend combined with a good country hook and some good engaging licks happening deep down in the mix. PICK OF THE WEEK MARTINA MCBRIDE "My Baby Loves Me" (RCA 07863) The first cut from her sophomore album. The Way That I Am, "My Baby Loves Me" gives all the evidence needed to cast Martina McBride as one of country's "next big things." An uptempo country tune written by Gretchen Peters and produced by Paul Worley, Ed Seay and McBride, "My Baby Loves Me" has hit single written all over it. Already a hit video, look for this one to grab hold of radio and not let go.

CASH BOX AUGUST?, INTERNATIONAL NEWS FROM JAPAN ACCORDING TO A SURVEY conducted by JVA (Japan Video As- sociation), the total shipments of video softwares here for May, 1993 were $154 million, 11.7% down from the comparable month of 1992 while the volume was 3,077,435 units, a 9% drop. Cassettes were $98 million, 64.3% of the total and 3.2% down which represented a volume of 1,767,663 units, 57.4% of the total and 3.4% down. Video disks took in $55 million, 35.7% of the total while dropping 23%. Cassette volume was 1,309,772 units, 42.6% of the total, 15.5% down for the period. Of the total units of cassettes, new works were 386 units in volume, up 2.9% while new video disks were 236 units, 2.6% up. The total units of new video software works were 622 units, 2.8% up over the month stated above. LOCAL 45s TOP 10 TW LW 1 - KOISEYO OTOME (Toshiba-EMI). Wands 2 4 DATTE NATSUJANAI (Sony).. T-Bo lan 7 - SMAP 004 (Victor)...SMAP 8 - INSANITY AND GENIUS (Victor). . .Ganma Lay 9 5 TORINO TOBIRA (Toshiba EMI)...Wands 10 - EYES (Toshiba EMI). ..Original Love BRAZIL By Christopher Pickard Shabba Ranks: Cornin' to Brazil RIO DE JANEIRO—Brazil's biggest media star and recording artist in recent years, Xuxa, is currently in Los Angeles where she is recording her first ever English language TV series for MTM (Mary Tyler Moore). While Xuxa has been hard at work on her English and the recording of her series, her manager, Marlene Mattos, has also been far from idle and has managed to scoop the pot by signing both Michael Jackson and Madonna for shows in Brazil at the end of the year. Despite having no experience in concert promotions, other than Xuxa's occasional live appearances, Mattos saw off bids from other established Brazilian promoters, thanks to her star's personal contact with Jackson. Jackson is set to play Rio de Janeiro, and possibly Sao Paulo, in October while Madonna is expected to follow in November if Mattos can organize a group of sponsors to bank the show. Jackson already has the backing of Pepsi Cola for his tour. Both artists will also play Argentina where the tours are being supervised by the experienced promoter, Daniel Grimback. It is not known what part TV Globo, to whom Xuxa is contracted in Brazil, will play in the tours or if any television specials will result from the concerts, but Rio's Maracana Stadium, the world's largest, has already hosted telecasts for Frank Sinatra, Sting, Tina Turner and Paul McCartney, all of whom set world boxoffice records for the largest paying crowd to see a single artist. The current record, cited in the Guinness Book of Records is for Paul McCartney, who performed to a crowd in excess of 180,000 on April 21, 1990. Maracana was also the site of Rock in Rio in 1991 when a crowd estimated to be closer to 200,000 packed the stadium for the night when Guns 'n Roses were the head- lining act. Prior to the arrival of Jackson and Madonna, Brazil will have the chance to see both Liza Minnelli and Shabba Ranks who are due in for shows in August while September sees the, by now, traditional Free Jazz Festival, South America's most important. This year the festival takes place in Rio at the theater of the Hotel Nacional from September 22 through 28 while in Sao Paulo Free Jazz will be based at the Palace from September 23 through 30. As in the past, the organizers have pulled together a collection of talent which any jazz festival would be proud of. Among the main international attractions set to play are Sade, Pat Metheny, Gerry Mulligan, Betty Carter, Joe Henderson, McCoy Tyner, Elvin Jones and Ornette Coleman. Free Jazz will also have its traditional blues night which this year brings to Brazil Bo Diddley and Clarence "Gatemouth" Brown. Another festival highlight will be a tribute to Brazil's Tom Jobim which unites Herbie Hancock, Gerry Mulligan, Jon Hendricks, Joe Henderson, Freddie Hubbard and Shirley Horn. Tickets go on sale in Brazil on August 7 and vary between $20 and $30.

CASH BOX AUGUST 7, 1993 8 NEWS/JAZZ Imagine... Lennon Exhibit To Tour Nationwide By Joseph Stanley RICK STEINBERG, OWNER OF NASHVILLE’S IMAGINE GALLERY has announced that, as a result of a special licensing agreement with the John Lennon Estate and its executrix Yoko Ono, an exhibit of original artwork and limited edition signed prints by Lennon will begin making appearances in selected cities throuhout the U.S. and Canada. The tour is scheduled to begin in late August, and will include photographs of Lennon by renowned photographer Bob Gruen. Steinberg has appointed Chicago native Tracy Nicol as special promotions director for the tour. Nicol has worked in the entertainment industry in Chicago, New York, London and Nashville since her graduation from Chicago's Columbia College. "I see this as a great opportunity to share with others a part of John Lennon that they might not know existed," says Nicol. 'The peace and love that Lennon tried to communicate in his music is just as evident—if not more so—in these works of art depicting his family and the world around him." For a personalized tour of the Nashville gallery or to obtain infor- mation about bringing the exhibit to your part of the country contact Tracy Nicol at (615) 662-0550. Also, private, after-hours showings of the gallery are available by appointment. Campbell Benefit Set FRIENDS AND FELLOW MUSICIANS will gather to pay tribute to blues great John Campbell, who died June 13 in New York. The event will take place at the Lone Star Roadhouse, where Campbell was a frequent performer, on August 6. Proceeds will go to the Paris Campbell Fund, to benefit his six-month-old daughter. Among those scheduled to perform are Dr. John, Jimmie Dale Gil- more, John Popper (of Blues Traveler), Chris Whitley, Campbell's back- ing band Cruel 13 and special guests Voodoo Children. For further information, please contact Lisa Milman at (310) 288- 3809 or the Lone Star Roadhouse at (212) 245-2950, or write to Paris Campbell Fund, c/o Fred Gobic, 530 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10021. Martinez STRAIGHT AHEAD: Body &Soul (Atlantic Jazz 782492-2). Producer. Lenny White. There's greater ensemble comfort on this album than on the Atlantic Jazz debut by this quintet of Motor City jazzists. The violin lead work by Regina Carter, the bass textures by Marion Hayden-Banfield, the pithy flute fills by Cynthia Dewberry, Gayelynrt McKinney's steady work on drums and Eileen Orr's subtle key work are given historical credibility on a trio of traditional tracks including the title track. On the contemporary material, the quintet explores gentle and rigorous tex- tures, especially on the lilting "Never Let You Go" and the post- fusionesque "Look Straight Ahead." A special treat is the Jam, Lewis and Hines-penned "Optimistic," which should spark airplay the way it did the Sounds of Blackness. a JOHN BEASLEY: A Change Of Heart (Windham Hill/BMG 01934 10145-2). Producer Walter Becker. There's plenty of attitude on this d isc, a 1 0-song collection that serves as a calling card for John Beasley's fresh piano attack. He's joined on the album by some of the best contemporary players around, including drummer Terri Lynne Carrington, percussionist Bill Summers, bassists John Patitucci and Freddie Washington, reedman Bob Sheppard and John Tavaglione, supplying some tasty alto and soprano sax leads. Beasley takes full advantage of the remarkable rhythm accompaniment on this album (like on the tracks "Carnal Appetite" and "Skippy") and finds more casual territory to accompany sidemen solos, like on "Until Now." There's not a boring moment on this disc.

Boyd (Acuff-Rose Music, Careas BMG Music Publishing Co., BMI/BMG Songs, Mickey Hitler Music, ASCAP 19 YOUR TIGHT RUIN' JEANS J Barnett (Young Graham Music, BMI) 67 REVIEWS by Brad Hogue GARTH BROOKS "Ain't Going Down (Til The Sun Comes Up)" (Liberty DPRO-79795) The lead single from his forthcoming Liberty CD Pieces is absolutely riotious! A screaming Chuck Berry- style guitar blazes through this line-danceable country kicker while excellent harmonica work howls and howls and howls. Hallelujah praise the Garth- man for breaking new ground with almost every single. Written by G.B. with Kent Blazy and Kim Williams, this one should hit #1 and stay a couple of weeks. Allen Reynolds produces. RICKY VAN SHELTON "A Couple Of Good Years Left" (Columbia CSK 77130) This is a fitting title since it's from Ricky Van's first studio album in two years titled A Bridge I Didn't Bum. The tune is a mid-tempo ballad about a growing adult relationship that's still got "A Couple Of Good Years Left." Written by Gary Burr and produced by Steve Buckingham, Snelton's super-strong vocal carries most ot the weight here with a soothing steel guitar adding even more strength. It's nice but not quite as exceptional as Van Shelton's other hits. KATHY MATTEA "Listen To The Radio" (Mer- cury CDP 879) From her Lonesome Standard Time release, "Listen To The Radio" was written by folk diva Nanci Griffith and interpreted confidently by Kathy Mattea. Upbeat and uplifting as radio itself, the tune combines great folk storytelling with modem country production from producer Brent Maher. There's nothing on the air exactly like this right now, so it should fit in quite nicely. Good stuff for the summer-! TURNER NICHOLS "Moonlight Drive-In" (BNA BDJ62577-2) The latest BNA signee. Turner Nichols is Zack Turner and Tim Nichols. "Moonlight Drive-In" is an extreme- ly well-written tune from the forthcoming release of tne same name. It puts you back in time when things were simpler and love was all-consuming. Written by Tumer/Nichols and Billy Kirsch with Keith Stegall producing, the song is certainly hot enough to garner these newly signed guys some well-deserved atten- tion. More good stuff for the summer! PICK OF THE WEEK MARY-CHAPIN CARPENTER "The Bug" (Columbia CSK 77134) Radio's gonna love this! It's difficult to even be critical of a tune that makes you feel as happy as this one does. Written by guitar legend Mark Knopfler, "The Bug" is a get-in-your-car and break-the-speed-limit-just-for-the-fun-of-it type of tune. Tempt the fates and get ready for another hit, 'cause Mary-Chapin's gonna take this one to the top. John Jennings and Steve Buckingham produced, with Carpenter also wearing a production hat.

Hogue LEE ROY PARNELL "On The Road" (Arista ASCD-2588) The first single from his forthcoming Arista CD. "On The Road" is a fine tip of the hat for those with a traveling bone. Written by Bob McDill, the mid-tempo tune glorifies the highway for a disgruntled wife, an anxious teenager, and even an old couple that wants to see a little more life. Parnell's vocals are strong and full, with Scott Hendricks producing. DEBORAH ALLEN "All The Loving And The HurtingToo" (Giant/Wam er Bros. PRO-CD-6355) Love hurts when only one's in love. That’s the theme from Deborah Allen's latest called "All The Loving And The Hurting Too." Co-written by Allen and Rafe VanHoy, the subtle ballad blends melodic keys with Allen's lead for a strong, believable stab at human heartache. From her Giant Records debut. Delta Dreamland, VanHoy produces with Allen acting as co-producer. MICHAEL WHITE "Country Conscience" (Reprise/Wamer Bros. PRO-CD-6204) This one borders on overkill, with too many references made about being "country." From White's forthcom- ing Reprise release, "Country Conscience" was writ- ten by White with Roger Murrah and Keith Stegall, with Stegall also producing. The two-stepping honky- tonker is complete with whining fiddle and strong White vocals, Dut the lyrics could use a little more work. STEPHANIE DAVIS "All In The Heart" (Asylum) The beauty in this debut Asylum single from Stephanie Davis is its straight-anead honesty. With simple lyrics written by Davis, "All In The Heart" gives just enough sentimentality to avoid being sappy. From her forthcoming Asylum debut, the summer ballad was produced by Kyle Lehning. Also, opening for Garth Brooks this year should put Davis in front of the audience she needs. PICK OF THE WEEK CLINT BLACK "No Time To Kill" (RCA 07863) The title cut from his smash album, "No Time To Kill" does nothing but insure Black's reputation as a powerhouse writer. The sense of contemporary urgency contained in this song is incredibly accurate and even picturesque, conjuring multitudes of images in the mind of its listener. Written with longtime writing partner Hayden Nicholas with James Stroud and Black producing, this one's not!

CASH BOX AUGUST 21, 1993 18 ARTIST SPOTLIGHT Paul Hardcastle By M.R. Martinez PAUL HARDCASTLE HAS ALWAYS GONE WITH HIS IN- STINCTS. And on his new JVC album. The Jazz Masters, the British- based musician instinctually plies the gentle waters of dance/pop/ jazz, which has earned him solid sales in Japan, critical acclaim and chart success in the U.S., but only mild interest in his homeland. "I knew going in that this record was not geared for Britain," Hardcastle told Cash Box during a trans-Atlantic phone in- terview. "It doesn't have a gimmick to it, which seems to be what many of the bands in England are forced to do. I don't do gimmicks, I do music." What Hardcastle has accomplished is a synthesis of his patented dance-oriented grooves with smoothed-out, gentle jazz textures that have optimized radio airplay and given the former Direct Drive member a spectrum of platforms from which to spring. While some fans of previous solo hits such as the dance floor hit "19" (which he composed, played on and produced) and "Rainforest," as well as hits for Ian Drury and the Blockheads ("Hit Me With Your Rhythm Stick" and "Reasons To Be Cheerful") may be curious, Hajdcastle takes a different view. He will now be identified with the single "Sound Of Summer," which may become a seasonal evergreen in retro rotation at many adult contem- porary stations. "I guess my audience has grown up with me," he says. The trans- formation may have begun when Hardcastle released a pair of albums for Chrysalis, including the slightly jazz-flavored, self-titled debut, and the follow-up No Winners. The former stereo-salesman-tumed-synth- player says the new album features co-production and flute and sax work of Gary Barnacle and the sensuous vocals of Helen Rogers. 'The album basically came out of Gary and I doing sessions in my studio, where we spent a lot of time experimenting, basically doing what we wanted," Hardcastle recalls. 'There was no record company to interfere with us." Hardcastle says that the album originally started out as an in- strumental, "but Helen was a friend of mine, and I thought that she would be perfect for some of the tracks." He says that Jeff Lunt, who handles promotion for JVC was the conduit for The Jazzmasters release through that company. He also mentioned Allen Kepler and Cody Leach as the people who helped make the record a success. "It's already gold in Japan, and we're closing in on solid sales in other markets." The record managed to remain a mainstay on several U.S. jazz, dance and R&B charts through the first months of the summer, with the single receiving wide airplay and record sales being spurred by a promotional tour upon which Hardcastle embarked in the late spring. In fact, after visiting Dallas radio station KAOI, Hardcastle, members of a local promotion team and radio staff were standing outside when they heard the sound of gunfire. "I stood there while everybody else dropped to the ground," he recalls. "I thought they were filming a segment of Cops! nearby. But it was the real thing." A lot like his music. Martinez U MILES DAVIS & QUINCY JONES: Live At Montreaux (Warner Bros. 9 45221-2). Producer Q. Jones. This dream session, recorded July 8, 1991 at the 25th anniversary of the Montreaux fest, finds Miles returning to one of his earlier incarnations of jazz primarily medleys and entries from his albums Miles Ahead, Porgy And Bess and Sketches Of Spain. Miles plays with spirit throughout the proceedings, and Quincy conducts the Gil Evans Orchestra and the George Gruntz Concert Jazz Band with a tender hand, staying true to Evans' arrangements, which made the original recordings sparkle. Soloists Kenny Garrett (alto saxophone) and Wallace Roney (trumpet/fluglehorn) provide some fresh inter- pretation for some of the work. RON CARTER: Friends (Blue Note CDP 0777 7 89548 28). Producer Ron Carter. Classical music and jazz often become different hues on a sound spectrum. While jazz allows for a more democratic interpretation of a composition, classical music is often played strictly in the spirit of the composer. Unless you're Ron Carter, and you decide to take pieces by Rachmaninoff, Chopin and Faureand put fresh stank on them. Joined by the venerable Kenny Barron (piano), Hubert Laws (flute) and a host of other sidemen. Carter brings a spring breath of fresh air to some venerable material—without sacrificing the history of the compositions. The title track (composed by Carter) fits in the mix easily.

CASH BOX AUGUST 21, 1993 30 COIN MACHHE By Camille Compasio AROUND THE ROUTE LET’S START WITH AN UPDATE on video gaming in the state of Illinois. Will it be legalized or not? The current edition of Coin Drop, the Illinois Coin Machine Operators Association publi- cation, presents a very convincing stance in favor of passage. Even the most hard-nosed legislator should be impressed with the projected revenue video gaming could generate for the state, by comparison to such other entities as riverboats, racing/OTB and bingo, to name a few. There has been no let-up at all in the efforts of ICMOA (via appearances before the House Task Force on Gaming and the Senate Subcommittee on gaming—which were well received), video gaming committee chairman Ray Shroyer, lobbyists Zack Stamp and John O'Connell; the latter having recently resumed his role after voluntarily stepping down when the committee's finances dipped. Representative Larry Hicks (D-Mt. Vernon), who has been working on this issue for five years, is optimistic that passage could come either at the special summer legislative session that was called because of the Chicago school crisis, or during the fall veto session. ICMOA, et al, have been conducting a very convincing program in behalf of their case and it has been attracting encouraging response on the part of legislators. Progress has been made in the formation of a coalition and meetings with influential groups and commercial entities are being held to strengthen the issue. A stronger call to action has been initiated by the association, urging ICMOA mem- bers to continue their support, both financially and through petitions, so that passage of the bill to legalize video gaming in Illinois can become a reality by next year. A REEAALLY BIG SHOW! We're talkin' about AMOA Expo '93, which will be coming up Oct. 21-23 at the Anaheim Conven- tion Center in Anaheim, California. This one has "record- breaker" written all over it, according to AMOA's Fred Newton—with over 1,030 booths already sold to 250 companies! Can you imagine the line-up of equipment that will be featured, not to mention all of the other factors (including locale) that should really beef up attendance! LUCKY DAY! On Friday, August 13, AAMA hosted an open house to show off its new headquarters at 450 East Higgins Road (Suite 201) in Elk Grove, Illinois! SAD, SAD, SAD! The flood of '93 and the accompanying hardship on individuals and businesses just doesn't seem to stop. In many cases, operators have luckily been spared from the submergence of their business premises only to find that then- locations were hard hit. Equipment had to be removed, some- times by boat, as in the case of Mike Green of Green's Games in Jerseyville, IL, who managed to salvage some pieces before a levee broke but was forced to leave a pool table and shuffleboard behind. Even the locations that were untouched had to close down because of flooded roads that prevented accessibility. When I initially contacted ICMOA's Adonna German to get a handle on how the flood affected ICMOA members, it was too soon to give me a report, however, the ensuing two weeks produced the above and following feedback. Mark Harting of Schaffner Music in Alton, IL was unscathed but downtown Alton had three feet of water, three other towns in the area were completely submerged and many of his locations were severely hit by the flooding. Paul Hoffmeister of P & M Enterprises in Waterloo had to literally empty out several of his locations but, thankfully, all of his equipment was saved. Phil Rowan of D & R Amusement in Davenport was frantically removing games as the flood waters were nearing many of his locations. Again, he was able to salvage most of his equipment. The horrible flood of '93 has continued to take its toll. People have lost their homes; many businesses have perished. There will be so much to worry about in the aftermath of the flood. All we can do is hope and pray and provide whatever support we can for the victims of this disaster. Rowe Plans A ‘Great Time For All’ At September Distribs Meeting CHICAGO—Bring yourself, bring your spouse, bring your camera and all else that is needed for a fun-filled, yet productive, weekend in the company of your colleagues and Rowe officials. Rowe International's annual distributor meeting will take place from Thursday, September 9 through Saturday, September 11 at the Westin Resort in Hilton Head Island, SC. Festivities will begin immediately with a hospitality reception on Thursday evening in the Danner Ballroom. On Friday morning, the "ladies only" breakfast (now a 'regular' event on the agenda) will be held in the Hibiscus room. It will be followed by the business meeting and product presentation (including a continental break- fast) in the Savannah Foyer. Attendees will have a choice of either the Carolina Cafe or the Pelican Poolside for lunch on this day. Friday afternoon, again, offers a choice of activities for attending distributors. Will it be golf at the Old South Golf Links championship course; or tennis, perhaps, at the Port Royal Racquet Club? Or, a narrated tour of Hilton Head Island, on air-conditioned buses, winding up at the Lighthouse in Harbor Town? While in Harbor Town, guests will board the Vagabond for a short "cruise" across the Caliboque Sound to Daufuski Island to meet the local inhabitants and experience a taste of true low country Southern cooking. Fridayevening will offcra tripdownmemorylaneat 'The Rock&Rowe Hop." A continental breakfast will take place Saturday morning, preceding the resumption of the business meeting, following which the "prin- cipals only" meeting and luncheon will be held. Climaxing event will be the annual Awards Banquet on Saturday evening. InterTainment ’93 Set For November In Santa Monica CHICAGO—-InterTainment '93, the international conference on inter- active entertainment, will present a most comprehensive look at the new media and the forces that are shaping it. The three-day event, the fifth since its inception, will be held November 3-5 at the Loew's Santa Monica Hotel in Santa Monica, California and is produced by Alexander & Associates, Inc., the New York-based business and market planning firm for the new media and entertainment industries. The conference agenda will feature general sessions, breakout panel discussions and demonstrations of the latest and most engaging ex- amples of interactive programming. Areas covered will include video, computer and CD-ROM games, children's programming, on-line com- munities, public place attractions, interactive television and interactive multimedia publishing. InterTainment '93 general sessions will be designed to help atten- dees break through the clutter of today's interactive technologies. In one, experts from various "converging media" (i.e. cable TV, computer services, telephone companies) will discuss the opportunities presented by the new technologies. In another, independent expert industry analysts will provide assessments of the viability and expected penetrations of different interactive media. "We think the time has come to separate the reality and oppor- tunities of interactivity from the hype," explained Robert C. Alexander, president of Alexander & Associates, which has run the InterTainment conferences since 1988. "A recent survey article referred to this industry as a 'vague new world'—but it's only vague if you're not up to date on what entertainment programmers are doing that works interactively." Sally Plourde, Alexander & Associates vice president and conference director, noted, "When we held our first conference five years ago, the concept of virtual reality was barely known outside NASA labs, video games were still 8-bit and Tamara, the interactive play, was just opening in New York. Today, interactive multimedia productions are delivered profitably on CD-ROMs, members of interactive on-line communities engage in on-line flight simulation games and new movie theaters are opening that give the audience a role in the film." These rapid but fundamental changes and developments in technol- ogy and products are shaping a whole new industry, according to Alexander. "InterTainment '93 participants will identify new and tan- gible business opportunities in this rapidly evolving field," he said, "because they'll see more clearly where the emerging consumer demand for interactive services really lies." Reservation forms and further information may be obtained from Alexander & Associates, 38 East 29th Street, 10th floor. New York, NY 10016. The phone number to call is 212-684-2333.

CASH BOX AUGUST 28, 19&3 i TALENT REVIEW TALENT REVIEW Tina Turner By Brad Hogue L.A. Philharmonic/ Kreizberg/Grimaud By Fred L. Goodman HOLLYWOOD BOWL, HOLLYWOOD, CA—What better way to spend a beautiful midsummer night in L.A. than at the Bowl with Glinka, Rachmaninov and Dvorak providing the delectable music. Add to the mix the L.A. Philharmonic with guest conductor Yakov Kreizberg and pianist Helene Grimaud, and in it you have a close-to-perfect concert experience. The orchestra opened with the sprightly Overture, Russian and Lud- milla by Glinka, which featured the 24-year-old Russian conductor's crisp direction. When France's Ms. Grimaud took the stage, one could sense from her confident entrance, that the crowd would be in a for a treat. She performed Rachmaninov's Piano Concerto No. 2 with tenacity and taste. Her flying fingers embraced the keys as if she were falling in love with the piece for the first time. The concerto itself has become a veritable "hit parade" medley of love songs, including the pop stand- ards "Full Moon And Empty Arms," and Eric Carmen's "All By Myself." Well-known melodies also abound in Dvorak's Symphony No. 9 (From the New World), the most recognizable being from the "Largo" Second Movement that became the black spiritual, "Goin' Home." The symphony is always a crowd-pleaser and on this night drew whoops and hollers from the usually laid-back L.A. audience. On a surreal note: For a few minutes during the Rachmaninov concerto, the orchestra and pianist were joined by an impromptu chorus of baying Hollywood Hills coyotes (or was it werewolves?). 'Tull Moon And Empty Arms" indeed! TALENT REVIEW Long Beach Jazz Festival STARWOOD AMPHITHEATRE, NASHVILLE, TN—All there is to say is WOW! When the lights dimmed after opening act Chris Isaac's show ended, signaling the sold-out crowd of 14,000 that the moment they'd all been waiting for was at hand, superstar entertainer Tina Turner emerged from a cluster of lights hovering high above the stage, seemingly stepped out of the heavens to descend a huge mobile stair- case and did a two-hour show in Music City, U.S.A. Opening with a super-sultry version of "Steamy Windows," Turner was joined by a musical entourage complete with beautiful twin danc- ing girls half her age. Turner did much more than keep up. Tirelessly blazing through hits from her 30-year career, the lady with legs brought new life to smash hits such as "Typical Male," 'Trivate Dancer" and "We Don't Need Another Hero," rollicked through the autobiographi- cal blues with "Nutbush City Limits," covered Robert Palmer's "Ad- dicted To Love," addressed the crowd as "Simply The Best," —discussed the fact that "I Don't Wanna Fight Anymore," engaged the crowd in a sing-a-long with "What's Love Got To Do With It," defined with total confidence the term "Proud Mary/' and encored with "Better Be Good To Me," then disappeared back into the same cluster of lights from which she gained entrance. Tina's total confidence and mesmerizing stage presence com- manded ovation after ovation. Fans and music industry types alike remained standing for practically the entire show. Lighting and choreography was second to none, and Turner made sure she thanked her entourage of traveling technical wizards, as well as her sensational band. As her What's Love tour continues to circle the globe. Turner can rest assured that none in attendance will ever forget her night in Nashville. Thanks to Virgin Records for the primo seats. It was in- credible! By M.R. Martinez RAINBOW LAGOON PARK, LONG BEACH, CA—The abun dance of styles was either a feast or famine for fans who attended this three-night, two-day jazz fest. If you were a jazz purist, then there was a respectable collection of highlights that would have satisfied such appetites, including the Friday set served up by veteran saxophonist Stanley Turrentine, whose tone and attitude was as fresh as some of the fusion work served up the following day. On Friday night, in contrast to Turrentine's set, Randy Crawford came with a more bluesy closing that was equally as exciting to those who have been fans of her vocal work over the years. A similar pairing was scheduled on Saturday night when Freddie Hubbard came on before Chaka Khan lit up the stage with her verbal pyrotechnics. Unlike his contemporary Turrentine, Hubbard was unable to establish a flow, and his truncated set was cooly received. Early on Saturday, acts such as Jeff Lorber, the Yellowjackets and Patrice Rushen (with Ndugu Chancier on drums and Neil Stubenhaus on bass) formed the core of a primarily electric set. Yellowjackets provided the most sting of the three. The mainstream offering of the day was an all-star aggregation featur- ing saxophonist Teddy Edwards with vocalists Ernie Andrews and Lorez Alexandria. Sunday was highlighted by the Latin percussion attack of Poncho Sanchez, who swapped for the closing spot with Lou Rawls. It was a fine strategic move, given that people left the Lagoon in a cheerful mood. Joining Sanchez and Rawls was former Crusader stalwart Wayne Henderson, Roy Ayers, Fattburger, legendary trumpeter Hugh Masekela and the opening all-star unit featuring the show's promoter, drummer A1 Williams.

COUNTRY SINGLES CASH BOX AUGUST 28, 1693 REVIEWS by Brad. Hogue m CLINTON GREGORY 'Master Of Illusion'' (Step One SOR-466) From his Step One CD of the same name, "Master Of Illusion" paints a vivid portrait of a man in love and also in denial of love. A soft tempo cut complete with keys, intricate guitar plucking and Gregory s melodic vocals, it was written by Mel Tillis, Jr. & Curt Ryle, with SOR prezzie Ray Pennington producing. I've said it before—Clinton Gregory pushes a little harder with each single release, and it shouldn't be long till he breaks wide open. JOHN ANDERSON "I Fell In The Water" (BNA 66232-2/4) The second single release from Anderson's Solid Ground album, 'T Fell In The Water" combines an upbeat stomp of a rhythm track with an excellent country hook: "/ fell in the water that you walked on." Written by Jerry Solley & Jeff Stevens, the country kicker should see immediate airplay on country radio, and it's surely a strong line-dancear>le number for the clubs. James Stroud produces with Anderson. SAMMY KERSHAW "Queen Of My Double Wide Trailer" (Mercury 314-514 332-2/4) She was fresh from the farm, and Sammy picked her up at Murphy' s restaurant, making her the 'Queen Of My Double Wide Trailer." Similar to the character in Brooks & Dunn's "Lost And Found" single, the queen in this tune is also hard to catch up with, and even more difficult to understand. Lots of strong country images are conjured in this song—one of Sammy s best to date. Written by Dennis Linde, the cut comes from Haunted Heart , and was produced by Buddy Cannon & Norro Wilson. Good stuff! BILLY BURNETTE "The Bigger The Love" (Capricorn 42007-2) First recorded by Lola Thomas on John McVie's Gotta Band project, "The Bigger The Love" showcases Billy Burnette s strong songwriting skills and demonstrates he's a contender in his field with a diverse, soulful voice. "/ should have picked on a love my own size,” Burnette says in the tune, which draws its strength totally from heartache and pain. Bluesy guitars and percussion coolness produced by Mark Wright just might push Burnette into his highest chart position yet. Give it a shot, radio. CONTEMPORARY CHRISTIAN CASH BOX SEPTEMBER 4, 199c' Newsboys— Nationwide ON AUGUST 13, 1993, THE NEWSBOYS were featured guests on Good Morning America, live from World Youth Day in Denver, Colorado. Interviewed for almost five minutes (the maximum time allotted for the show's celebrity interviews), host Joan Lunden quizzed the guys about their Australian and American backgrounds, but the interview took a wonderful spiritual turn. The group had the opportunity to explain how their faith has grown individually, ana how, in turn, the band has evolved and developed their music and their message. The message of the Newsboys is crystal-clear, proclaiming (especially to youth) that being a Christian is not a boring, underrated lifestyle, and that it doesn't necessarily involve giving money to a televangelist or living by some set of strict rules. The message the Newsboys present in their concerts, in their music, and on Good Morning America, plainly states that being a Christian is the most exciting lifestyle there is. The Newsboys interview was promoted throughout the hour prior to their appearance, and a clip from their #1 musicvideo, 'T Cannot Get You Out Or My System," was shown during the interview segment. In addition to this, Nashville's WAY-FM aired the interview live during their morning show. Response from the Good Morning America staff was great, with requests for CDs and interest shown in attending a Newsboys concert. Also, a very friendly Joan Lunden spent a good deal of time with the group prior to the interview. Good Morning America is the #l-rated morning show in the country. Later that day, the Newsboys performed for thousands of young people at Denver's Civic Center. Preparing for the Good Morning America live interview are(l-r): Jody Davis, guitar; Kevin Mills, bass; John James, lead vocals; Peter Furler, drums; and host, Joan Lunden. Tales Of Wonder Makes History STAR SONG COMMUNICATIONS recently threw a party for the mem- bers of White Heart, celebrating the radio success of their Grammy- nominated album. Tales of Wonder. Reportedly a first in Contemporary Christian Music radio, all 10 songs on the album were relesaed as singles, and all 10 charted! To date, the singles have gotten three #l's: "Say The Word,'— ' "His Heart Was Always In It," and "Silhouette." Three songs gained #2 status: "Unchain," "Raging Of The Moon," and "Light A Candle." There was one #4, "Vendetta," and a top 40, "Gabriella." The final two songs, "Who Owns You," and "Where The Thunder Roars" are currently working their way up the charts. White Heart's next album. Highlands, is due out in October. At the party (l-r) are: (Front row) Star Song radio promotions coordinator Jill Landess; White Heart lead singer Rick Florian. (Back row) W.H. drum- mer Jon Knox; W.H. keyboardist Mark Gersmehl; W.H. guitarist Brian Wooten: S.S. marketing manager, Jason Parker; W.H. guitarist Bill Smiley; S.S. marketing director, Mike Keil; S.S. vp marketing & sales, Danny McGuffey. Integrity For the Kids INTEGRITY MUSIC HAS ANNOUNCED the release of two new albums in the Scripture Memory Songs series. There is no better feeling on earth than to know that you are unconditionally loved. The first new release of Scripture Memory Songs, "God's Love," affirms the agape love God has for you. From the country sounds of "The Life I Live" to the contemporary jazz feel of "Within Your Temple," these 10 word-for-word Scripture songs paint a musical portrait of the consistent, steadfast, unfailing love of God. The catchy melodies help tuck away the truth of God's love deep in the heart with every Scripture-built lyric. Featured vocalists include Mike Eld red, Rita Baloche, Cathy Riso and Chris Rodriguez. After watching one broadcast of the evening news, one could easily be overcome by the realization that the world is not a pretty place. In fact, it can be downright scary. You can lose your job, your health, your family, have a wreck, etc. The list goes on and on of things we can be afraid of. That's where Overcoming Fear from Integrity's Scripture Memory Songs comes in. Tire songs on this release will strengthen and establish faith in times of trouble. Whether dressed in the lush orchestral backdrop of "There Is A River" or in the jazz groove of "Greater Is He," the comforting words of these 10 songs help fear subside, reassuring us that God is near and eager to help us. Finally, Rob Evans, the Donut Man, and the Donut Repair Club head for the Zoo on The Donut Repair Club At The Zoo, the new live action video from Integrity Music. The video weaves in a fast-paced storyline with singing, laughing, Duncan's humor, and a lot of animals. Filmed on location at the Dallas Zoo, The Donut Repair Club At The Zoo teaches kids about how God takes care of his creation, and how we should take care of each other. A double-value audio cassette version of the video is also being released. A1 Gore In Good Company BENSON’S NEW VOCAL GROUP, STRAIGHT COMPANY was recently invited to perform for Vice President A1 Gore at a family policy conference held in Nashville. The conference, called "Family Reunion II," was a day-long "kitchen-table" discussion of the pressures and needs of families, the values that drive family policy, and the current response to those needs by the public and private sectors. The conference, moderated by the Vice President, was held at the Tennessee Performing Arts Center. Straight Company, a uniquely talented a cappella group from Louisville, Kentucky, has already been creating quite a stir. Musi- cally, the group combines street-comer doo-wop, Caribbean calyp- so, gospel-tinged praise and worship, and hip-hop with creative vocal rhythyms and commercial hooks. Straight Company releases their debut Benson project. So Excited A Cappella, in September. Grammy and Dove Award-winning artists Sandi Patti and Steven Curtis Chapman teamed up recently in Nashville with producer Greg Nelso to put the finishing touches on “He Shall Feed His Flock,” one of their contribu- tions to the new Young Messiah recording. In addition to their duet, Steven and Sandi have solo recordings featured on the album and the new tour as well. The New Young Messiah releases September 13, with the tour starting later this fall.

REVIEWS CASH BOX SEPTEMBER 11, '3993 5 TALENT REVIEW Hollywood Bowl Orchestra w/ John Mauceri By S. K. Durham HOLLYWOOD BOWL, HOLLYWOOD, CA—Remember the good old days when you'd slide into a plush seat in the center of an cavernous movie theater decorated like a baroque birthday cake? Remember hugging an ice cold Coke and a large bucket of salty, buttered popcorn, and waiting impatiently for the lights to go out so the movie magic could electrify your senses? Remember? Last Friday night the full house at the Hollywood Bowl came to remember, and have their senses electrified. Great Scenes and Music From Classic Films performed by the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra and conducted by John Mauceri, honored some of the finest film score composers of Hollywood's golden era and at the same time co-mingled our collective memories. A massive movie screen stretched the length of the stage above the orchestra. On this screen flashed classic images from master- print movie clips. Clips with the original voice track only—no sound effects, no soundtrack, no score. Mauceri and the orchestra added the movie score the old-fashioned way—live, in sync and seamless—equipped only with a simple timing device and a small monitor to follow the action. A guy sitting behind us exclaimed with great conviction that John Mauceri was a "bitchin' " conductor. As the night progressed I had to agree. Mauceri, in a deep resonant voice, introduced each piece of music with reverence and humor, letting the audience in on interesting little secrets about the composers and their music. His conducting style was kinetic. He would move from graceful controlled direction to leaps in the air as high as a foot-ana-a-half. Movie music spotlighted included Eric Komgold's Adventures Of Robin Hood, Bernard Herrmann's Citizen Kane and North By Northwest, Miklos Rosza's Madame Bovary and Ben-Hur, and Max Steiner's Gone With The Wind. One hopes Mauceri and orchestra will make the "Movie Music" concert an annual event. Don't miss them next time, "they're bitchin'." TALENT REVIEW JVC Jazz By Brad Pressman HOLLYWOOD BOWL, HOLLYWOOD, CA—Only one way to describe this evening at the famed Hollywood Bowl...PERFECT! For those of us who listen to and follow the movers and shakers in Contemporary Jazz, you just couldn't ask for a better concert. O.K., here's the line-up: 6:00 p.m. - the lovely keyboardist Keiko Matsui with special guests Greg Walker (formerly with Santana) and hus- band Kazu, a brilliant "shakuhachi" player. 7:30 p.m. - Fourplay featuring four of the best (and I really mean the best) Contemporary Jazz musicians of the modem scene.. .Lee Ritenour, Bob James, Harvey Mason and Nathan East! 9:00 p.m. - The soulful saxophonist from Buffalo, Grover Washington, Jr. Not only was this a great line-up to begin with, but also a beautiful evening in the Hollywood Hills apart from the daily rut of L.A. Keiko Matsui played a variety of hits from her six albums (the first of which was recently re-released A Drop Of Water). Her newest release. Cherry Blossom, topped the charts earlier this year, and Matsui thanks the fans for letting her continue to do what she loves. ..play music. Dressed to impress, Matsui seemed very com- fortable in front of such a big audience; and her guest vocalist Greg Walker reveled in the fact that he was there on stage as opposed to being in the audience where he sat as an L.A. youth. Now things really got moving when the new "Fabulous Four," Fourplay, hit the stage for a jazz lover's delight, a mixture of hits from their two albums. The set featured exciting upbeat hits like "Bali Run" and the NAC radio hit "Max-O-Man" as well as a few tracks from their latest effort Between The Sheets. Nathan East provided the vocals for this mostly instrumental quartet which sounded like a full orchestra instead of four men on a huge stage. Between The Sheets is a great follow-up album to the debut; and fans were so taken by the band's first L.A. performance that they demanded one encore song after the set. The song was "After The Dance," a vocal track from album #1 that originally featured singer El DeBarge. Grover time! As one radio announcer so eloquently said recently, "Saxophonists come and go. ..but Grover is here to stay" (or some- thing to that effect). The point is, this guy has been delighting Contemporary Jazz lovers for so many years that one sometimes forget to pull out that CD of his that's been collecting dust. He's been recording since the '70s, following a brief tour in the Vietnam War where he was fortunately stationed away from combat areas. But 1980 was the year Grover Washington, Jr. became a (Jazz) household name with his Grammy-winning album Winelight, which of course featured the hit single "Just The Two Of Us." That song also won a Grammy and featured the talented vocalist Bill Withers. During one song, Grover and the gang broke into a "sample- fest" of hip hop sounds that the audience both recognized and appreciated. The most popular track they borrowed was Wrecx-N- Effect's "Rumpshaker" which got lots of people out of their seats. What a great idea. ..mix some groovin' hip-hop beats with some bust-out Jazz, and you've got an explosive sound that no one expected. After all, what's wrong with mixing two types of music? Some would argue they like crossover music as much as any one format, and the musicians really prefer not to be labeled anyhow. Grover's latest release. No Exit, is definitely hot and worth picking up but first find that old Grover album, dust it off, listen to it and then try to catch him live. This guy could very well be the king of a new format..."FUNK-JAZZ?!" TALENT REVIEW Everly Brothers/Dion By Fred L. Goodman GREEK THEATRE, LOS ANGELES, CA—The Baby Boomers were out in force last Sunday at the Greek as two of rock 'n' roll's seminal acts took the stage for a rollicking evening of "oldies but greaties." The Everly Brothers and Dion, all members of the Rock 'N' Roll Hall of Fame, performed their evergreens to an appreciative audience of middle-aged, but young-at-heart die-hards. Bronx boy Dion opened the bill with a slew of his streetwise classics including "Drip Drop," "Donna The Prima Donna," "Ruby Baby," "A Teenager In Love" and "The Wanderer." An a cappella version of "I Wonder Why" (his first hit with the Belmonts) was a standout, as well as a touching reading of his 1968 smash, "Abraham, Martin & John." A rousing "Runaround Sue" (his biggest and most enduring hit) served as the finale. While Dion was busting the charts with those urban-tinged paeans of teenage angst during the late '50s and early '60s, the Everly Brothers were the more rural side of the coin. Their Ken- tucky/Nashville roots, evident in their more countrified take on young love, were very apparent this night, even to the point of adding pedal steel guitar to the mix. The tighter-than-tight sibling harmonies were still there on such hits as "Bye Bye Love," "Wake Up Little Susie," "All I Have To Do Is Dream," "When Will I Be Loved" and "Till I Kissed You." It is with such songs as "Cathy's Clown" and "Crying In The Rain" that one hears the Everlys' influence on all that followed, especially the Beatles. They finished with a sublimely sensitive "Let It Be Me," arguably one of the most beautiful love songs of the rock era. Dion and the Everly Brothers prove that rock 'n' roll, '50s style or otherwise, will never, ever die. The Everlys: Phil (I) and Don

Barnett (Young Graham Music, BMI) 67 REVIEWS by Brad Hogue RICK TREVINO "Just Enough Rope" (Columbia CSK 77159) Expect Columbia to explore a few cross-marketing strategies with this Johnny Rodriguez-influenced Texas newcomer named Rick Trevino. A third generation Mexican-American, Trevino grew up playing to, and straddling two cultures in the suburbs of Austin and Houston, "just Enough Rope" is the debut single from his forthcoming Columbia album. Written by Karen Staley & Steve Dean, the tune is a pleasing mid-tempo shuffle with a cool for radio. Can't wait to hear the Spanish version. Steve Buckingham produced the track. ALABAMA "Reckless" (RCA 07863) From their forthcoming RCA CD, The Cheap Seats, "Reckless" was written by Jeff Stevens & Michael Clark with production handled by Josh Leo, Larry Michael Lee & Alabama. It's a mid-tempo tune about driving down the road in reckless summer love. Typi- cal Alabama harmonies are tight as ever and thesong's not bad, but it's nothing spectacular—by Alabama standards anyway. ALAN JACKSON "Mercury Blues" (Arista 18711) While it's hard to follow the success of a single like "Chattahoochee," this one just might be the ticket to sell a few more albums. Written by Robert L. Geddins & K.C. Douglas, "Mercury Blues" demonstrates in ditty an ongoing love affair with a brand-name automobile. We have to hand it to Alan for demonstrating diverse interests in his single releases. It's produced by Keith Stegall. HIGHWAY 101 "You Baby You" (Liberty DPRO-79858) They're back as strong as ever. "You Baby You" is the much-anticipated single from Highway 101's new Liberty CD, A New Frontier. With an off-beat rhythm and a great vocal mixture, the song is pressed in super-cool Appalachian twang and turbo-charged with an energetic production of lively fiddle, slammin' drums and a large group chorus. LITTLE TEXAS "God Blessed Texas" (Warner Bros. PRO-CD-6448) It's about time for this one! We all knew they could something besides weepy ballads and here it is. "God Blessed Texas" is a smashing new single that is sure to take radio by storm. Written by Porter Howell & Brady Seals of (he band, this is the best single our Little band has released to date. It's an end-of-summer, honky-tonk stomp wonderfully produced by James Stroud, Christy DiNapoli & Doug Grau. Take it to the masses, guys!

But Chris- tian music's best kept secret isn't keeping quiet anymore. With the group's first Christmas release. Season of Love, due out in October, a secured spot on the much- sought-after, hot Young Messiah project and a 25-city tour scheduled for the fall, Mark Harris, Kirk Sullivan, Andy Chrisman, and Marty Magehee are staring straight down at a busy and successful fall schedule. 4HIM's soft pop-rock quartet sound has made the band a favorite to a surprisingly diverse audience. While the industry has been slow to jump on the band's fan wagon, consumers young and old have been flocking to the group's energetic, if not homogeneous, live performance. Melodic four-part harmonies and lush arrangements with enough guitar to make the music pop, 4HIM preaches and prods its audience with a decidely motivated, inspirational message. CASH BOX SEPTEMBER 18, 1993 4 INDUSTRY BUZZ By Aaron Steinberg McCoy Tyner: Performing with verve AFTER THE NEW YORK SALSA FESTIVAL took NYC into the wee-wee hours (with performances by Marc An- thony and Tito Nieves), the town found itself awash in the cool breeze of steel drums on Labor Day, as nearly a million and a half enjoyed the West Indian-American Day Carnival Parade, which concluded four days of celebration. Upstate in Saratoga Springs, Peter Gabriel spearheaded a batch of per- formances related to his WOMAD label. Among the par- ticipants were PM Dawn and Gabriel himself. OUR FAVORITE THINGS: McCoy Tyner and his trio closed out a weeklong stand at the Blue Note Sunday night before an enthusiastic SRO crowd. Tyner, though not the kind to while away the hours chatting with the audience, seemed in especially good spirits as he led his fired-up rhythm section through the set. He is thought of most readily, of course, as having been John Coltrane's pianist during the master's most acknowledged years, and today he has by no means aban- doned the modal (or one scale) concepts they explored. Not to suggest he isn't his own man; he has said that he was merely pursuing his own intentions on the piano and that they happened to coincide with Coltrane's seminal musings. TTiey began the show with Tyner's "Home," a piece that paired a more traditional section of swing changes with a single, modal vamp that gave bassist Avery Sharpe a chance to display his unusual (in the jazz world) approach to soloing: dirty blues phrases and slapping and popping on the upright bass. As he continued, he moved into strumming repeated guitar chords, intriguing the audience an extra notch. Continuing with a lightning-fast version of Coltrane's "Lazy Bird," they rounded out the set with a solo piece by Tyner that mixed bright, busy flourishes with sustained, moody moments. The untitled tune that followed seemed to focus the evening's best—African rhythms layered with Latin embellishments from drummer Aaron Scott provided a living foundation for Sharpe's single-line mantra, giving Tyner the space to take us out there. Together, they're a well-oiled unit, as one can hear on Tyner's Turning Point (Verve), a Grammy winner this year that finds the group holding down the fort for a big band performance. ON THE STREET WHERE YOU LIVE there might be more history than you realize—this week the part of Avenue B in Manhattan that adjoins Tomkins Square Park was named "Charlie Parker Place" (Bird had a brownstone there in his later years), commemorating the life of a musician whose relationship with the city was as nurturing as it was symbiotic and fateful. By Troy ]. Augusto A If; vUS£V. A 1 llSTv-z; K fftVSf ; >. •«>« l KIIS-FM hosted a M ' 2 L;i benefit for the L.A. M*"®' n : If Unified School ^ 9 District’s Performing ” Arts Program at the Palace. Musical performers included Inner Circle, Tag Team and SoCal reggae favorites Big Mountain. As if that wasn’t enough, the station hired a gaggle of celeb look-a-likes to shock and amuse the gathered folk. Seen here, (i-r), hamming it up at the party are a faux RuPaul (too short), station jock Rick Dees, false Madonna (too young), phony George Michael (too-fake beard) and flim-flam Janet Jackson (too big). A fake Heidi Fleiss was seen in front of the club scalping tickets. AS FOR THE REAL MTV AWARDS, the show had its ups and its definite downs. The evening's host, Hunk-of-the-Hour Christian Slater, turned in a workingmanlike effort, accept- able but hardly as entertaining as past hosts. Dare we say bring back Arsenio? At times stiff and too low-key, Slater was simply out of his element. There's no doubting the man's acting abilities—he's one of the most exciting young actors in Hollywood—but awards show hosting is definitely not some- thing Slater should include on his resume. The undisputed performance winner of the evening was the Neil Young/Pearl Jam jam on Young's "Rocking In The Free World," as unexpectedly arousing as anyone's ever been in the program's 10- year history. Other highlights included a moving turn from R.E.M. (when are they going to tour again?), Aerosmith's surprisingly potent rendition of "Living On The Edge," a new song from Pearl Jam (can't wait to hear the new album, due in mid-October) and this exchange, in the press tent, between k.d. lang and a male reporter: Reporter: "What was going through your mind when you did that Vanity Fair photo-shoot with Cindy Crawford?" lang: "Probably the same thing that would have been going through your mind!" Well said. Other backstage moments to cherish included Tony Ben- nett (new album soon) shaking hands outside the media port-a-potty area; members of the Red Hot Chili Peppers changing their clothes, post-show, in front of their dressing room's open windows, much to the delight of a group of giggling looky-loos; the number of clueless reporters that asked celeb's opinion on the Michael Jackson scandal (few commented); and evening-long speculation on whether rap- per Snoop Doggy Dogg (Calvin Broadus) would be able to elude police long enough to appear on the program with partner Dr. Dre. He did in fact manage to appear and then slip out of the area without being noticed by the boys in blue who were probably more interested in trying to get into the after-party. (Dogg has since been formally charged with mur- der stemming from a shooting August 25 that left one alleged gangmember dead. It's alleged that he was driving the vehicle that was carrying the triggerman, allegedly Snoop's bodyguard, McKinley Lee.) An odd onstage conversation took place between 7-foot drag queen/dance diva RuPaul and Milton Berle, whereby each seemed intent on insulting the other. Is this a great show or what? Kodak moments at the party included the appearance, in full costume, of Heather, the little girl in the bee suit from the front of the Blind Melon album, an unexpected appearance from injured tennis star Monica Seles, who wasn't in a talking mood, and the paparazzi crush that hounded Peter Gabriel and Sinead O'Connor as they tried to enter the shindig. MTV will be rerunning the entire awards show everyday until next spring, when the channel announces the participants for the 1994 show. Can't wait.

CASH BOX SEPTEMBER 18, 1993 16 It was a star-laced affair, featuring Oleta Adams at a special live listening session featuring songs from her new Fontana/Mercury Records album Evolution, some songs from her platinum-plus debut Circle of One. Some of the artists that showed for the event, held in early August included Wesley Snipes, Halle Berry, Tears For Fears leader Roland Orzabal, Debbie Allen, and pictured with Adams (above left) Rosie O’Donnell and Jody Watley. JAZZ7ADULT NOTES: Indie and /or boutique labels are making some noise in the land of Jazz, Adult Contemporary, New Age and World Beat. Labels such as Sin-Drome, Gyroscope, Earth- Beat/Wamer Bros., Lipstick, Windham Hill, Higher Octave, Mo- Jazz, Private Music and others are releasing such a dazzling array of adult, jazz-oriented and ethnic musics that it's becoming increas- ingly difficult to cubbyhole any of the music. Artists like Peter White and Jim Chapell whose respective Sin-Drome Records album Promenade and Real Music collection Over The Top have been chart staples in recent weeks, are but a pair of the artists of this ilk quietly adding to the cash flow at retail. Some product to keep an eye on includes the Gyroscope Records release of Laraaji's Flow Goes The Universe and Harold Budd's Music For 3 Pianos, both of which will make noise in the New Age market, and receive some adult airplay on some jazz stations. New releases on Windham Hill Records by Alex De Grassi, John Beasley, and Nightnoise will in varying degrees have an impact on the NAC market. DeGrassi's built-in following will move his record through the pipeline, Beasley's strong jazz album (including several star guest sidemen) will provide him some cash register fuel and the major tour by Nightnoise, with DeGrassi and formidable pianist Liz Story, will help with sell- through on this product. Blue Note recording artist Benny Green earned major kudos as the recipient of the prestigious City of Toronto Glenn Gould Internation- al Protege Prize in Music and Communication. On hand during the presentation to Green, whose fourth Blue Note album was recently released, was legendary jazz pianist Oscar Peterson, also a Gould winner. The awards are given out by Canadian-based Glenn Gould Foundation. Pictured are (l-r): Bassist Ray Brown; guitarist Herb Ellis; drummer Jeff Hamilton; John Hnatyshyn, Governor General of Canada; Green; and (seated) Peterson. Across The Borderline, "Still Is Still Moving ToMe" is a captivating little single strengthened by a Spanish-acoustic guitar mix, poetic lyrics and an upbeat Willie vocal which is as interpretive, strong, and powerful as ever. Written by the Red-headed Stranger himself, the Tex-Mex ditty employs a really fast-paced rhythm with a dis- tant crying steel that's gonna put you out there in another time or place if you listen closely and let the music do the talking. Don Was produced. area, - ff \ i \ SJr 00 JEFF KNIGHT "Easy Street" (Mercury CDP 977) A much stronger approach than his previous singles, "Easy Street" just might be the one to make people remember Jeff Knight s name. Written by T.J. Knight & Curtis Wright, the tune blends a haunting enough melody with the rich-man-poor-man theme which is so popular in country music today. It just might work if radio catches on soon enough. Bud Logan & Harold Shedd produced. CHRIS LEDOUX "Every Time I Roll The Dice" (Liberty DPRO-79002) His Liberty debut was a golden success thanks to Garth Brooks. Now let's see how LeDoux fares alone with "Every Time I Roll The Dice," the second single from his Under This Old Hat CD. Written by Max D. Bames & Troy Seals, the mid-tempo waltzer has cow- boy Chris singing with a cool country fiddle, accom- panying steel, and some well-placed lead licks. The lady in the song is likened to a card game, and "I'm holding on for dear life...” Jimmy Bowen & Jerry Crutchfield produced the track. pi ^ YA DARON NORWOOD "If It Wasn't For Her I Wouldn't Have You" (Giant PRO-CD-6447) This type of song has worked well in the past, so Giant's trying it again with Daron Norwood. "If It Wasn't For tier I Wouldn't Have You" says it all basically. J.L. Wallace & Terry Skinner wrote the tune of losing infatuation and finding real love. James Stroud & Jeff Carlton produced the light-hearted track. PICK OF THE WEEK DALE DANIEL "Coming Back To Haunt Me" (BNA 66283-2/4) Sultry, sexy and captivating. This one deserves some attention immediately! I haven't read her bio yet and don't know what she looks like as we go to print, but after listening to "Coming Back To Haunt Me," I'm a little haunted myself. From her BNA debut. Luck Of Our Own, this atten tion-grabbing tune was wri tten by Dale Daniel & Rick Bowles with Jerry Crutchfield producing. Excellent stuff—radio's gonna love it!

Boyd (Acuff-Rose Music, Careers BMG Music Publishing Co., BMl/BMG Songs, Mickey Hiller Music, ASCAP .5 REVIEWS by Brad Hogue MATTHEWS WRIGHT & KING "One Of These Days" (Columbia CSK 77180) From Dream Seekers, "One Of These Days" provides more of that M.W.K. group harmony to which we're becoming accustomed! Written by Billy Livsey & Don Schlitz, the tune delves into selfless rediscovery and happily presents an otherwise sadder subject. "One of these days l won't cry all night over you..." Produced by Randy Scruggs. Excellent track! CHRIS ISAAK "Solitary Man" (Reprise CDX Vol. #64) Looks like everyone wants apiece of country radio! Chris Isaak indeed does a fine job covering Neal Diamond's "Solitary Man/' but strangely enough, I've never seen him on TNN or CMT before. Given the success of Dwight Yoakam's recent epic, "A Thousand Miles From Nowhere," this forlorn tune just might gamer some airplay on cutting-edge country stations. Good stuff!Erik Jacobson produced. EVANGELINE "Still Loving You" (MCA/Mar- garitaville MCA5P-54747) They made quite an impressive debut last year, and Jimmy Buffet's wisdom in signing Evangeline to his Margaritaville label is quite apparent. Written by Stephen Allen Davis, "Still Loving You" presents vivid visual images of unrequited love and longing. Produced by Justin Neibank and Michael Utley of Coral Reefer fame, the track is primed for multi-for- mat airplay with vocals out front where they should be. Reminiscent of K.T. Oslin. From their forthcoming release, French Quarter Moon. Cool tune! PICK OF THE WEEK RADNEY FOSTER "Hammer And Nails" (Arista ASCD-2608) Good follow-up! "Hammer & Nails" sees Radney f etting strong vocally and rowdy on guitar. Written y Foster with Cindy Bullens, this upbeat barroom stomper was produced well by Steve Fishell & Foster. Multi-talented guy, huh? Look for this one to catch radio's attention and keep it for a while. Arista's had some good luck this year with Radney, so drive it on home. From Del Rio, TX 1959. CHARLIE FLOYD "I've Fallen In Love (And I Can't Get Up)" (Liberty DPRO-79001) It's a rare week when all those reviewed deserve Pick of the Week honors, but Charlie Floyd rises to the top this time with "I've Fallen In Love (And I Can't Get Up)." Written by Ronnie Samoset & Craig Wiseman and interpreted perfect- ly by Liberty^ latest hunk, this is a honky-tonk stomp ready for the dance halls. Country radio's gonna love it. Wear it out; it's a hit! Jimmy Bowen & Clyde Brooks produce.

CASH BOX OCTOBER 2, 1993 10 HEWS/JAZZ Monterey Becomes Eclectic Under New Leadership By M.R. Martinez MONTEREY, CA—A new era kicked off—and a previous epoch was paid tribute—with variety and competence at the 36th annual Monterey Jazz Festival presented by MCI, which featured several newcomers who served a cornucopia of sound on three separate stages on the Fairgrounds. With the departure last year of festival founder Jimmy Lyons (who was on hand for part of the three-night, two-day fest), there was an evident move toward broadening the bookings and attracting younger generations of fans for this annual event. Artists like McCoy Tyner, Les McCann, Eddie Harris, Clark Terry, Dr. John, the dirty Dozen Brass Band, Charles Lloyd and the Heath Brothers, shared the fresh festival air with young turks such as Alphabet Soup, the Santa Cruz Steel, Roy Hargrove, Antonio Hart, Todd Cochran Trio, Talking Drums, Sumi Tonooka Trio and Steve Turre. It was like choosing from a menu—the traditional Main Arena meal, crispy selec- tions from the Garden Stage and heady concoctions from the Nightclub. An added treat was that, except for headliners many of the artists in the Main Arena show served samplings at the other venues prior to their main performances. While there was the pleasing presence of new faces and sounds including modern steeWrum aggregations and hip-hop/ jazz acts some of the best performances during the fest were turned in by jazz veterans. Although new to the Monterey music confab, Les McCann & Eddie Harris fronting a quartet made the most of their crowd-pleasing set during the opening Friday night Main Arena show. The show also featured newcomers Bobby Watson & Horizon featuring Victor Lewis, Charlie Haden with his Liberation Music Orchestra and the Oakland Youth Chorus and Ruben Blades, who is reportedly eschewing his music career for pursuit of politics in his native Panama. McCann and Harris paced the Friday show with their funky jazz excusion into hits like "Compared To What" and McCann's causal irreverence with the audience. However, opening act Watson & Horizon got things off to a rousing start due to the engaging trumpet work of young turk Terell Stafford. Pianist Amina Claudine Myers took Haden's set to church with soulful singing, playing and accompani- ment by the Oakland Youth Chorus. Robin Eubanks completed the Haden package with some gripping trombone solo work. Blades, while his set alternated between Afro-Cuban cocktail fusion and kenetic effervescent salsa work, was a crowd-pleaser as a closer. As Blades closed the Main Arena, Bay Area-based, hip-hop/jazz aggregation Alphabet Soup served off some fresh sonic treats for the auditory palate on the Garden Stage. Highlights during the remaining four performances included Dr. John & The New Island Social & Pleasure Club in a Saturday matinee jambalaya of Cajun- flavored soul backed by the savory Mardi Gras- flavored marching band eclectism of the Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Barbara Boykins' articulate blues vocals on the Garden Stage during the matinee made a joyous noise. Saturday night's highlights were bountiful, with the Brccker Brothers featuring guitarist Mike Stern and drummer Lenny White in a blistering fusion set; Joe Williams turned in the kind of soulful set that he has made a staple offering whenever he's at the festival Monterey; and the McCoy Tyner Big Band with special guest Bobby Hutcherson gregariously ignited a bombardment of fresh playing of venerable themes. Sunday afternoon's set was paced by the home-run swing of the California High School All-Star Jazz Band with special guest Clark Terry and under the direction of Bill Berry and Paul Cantos. Boyd (Aculi-Rose Music, Careers BMG Music Pubfishing Co., BMI/BMG Songs, Mickey Hitter Musk, ASCAP 20 REVIEWS by Brad Hogue BILLY RAY CYRUS "Somebody New" (Mer- cury 314-514 758-2/4) You have to hand it to Cyrus for cutting great songs. This one instantly captivates with a super-cool bass line straight outta the Twin Peaks movies. Another tale of unrequieted love, "Somebody New" was written by Alex Harvey & Mike Curtis and produced by Joe Scaife & Jim Cotton. From the Mercury CD It Won't Be The Last, the mid-tempo melody here provides a strong backdrop for some really well-done harmonies. KELLY WILLIS "Heaven's Just A Sin Away" (MCA MCA5P-54733) All right! A good 'ol cheatin' song of old. (Remember the Kendalls?) Anyway, Kelly Willis gives a great interpreta tion of this Jerry Gillespie classic. The "woh- wohs" are in all the right places and Willis sounds like she's really having a tough time deciding what she'll do in the situation. To cheat or not to cheat, that is the question. From her MCA debut, Kelly Willis, Don Was & Tony Brown produced. DOUG SUPERNAW "I Don't Call Him Daddy" (BNA 66133-2/4) This is oneof thosesongsthatcould really touch the lives of many. Written by Reed Nielsen, the melodic ballad tells the story of a father's love for a son he rarely sees. From Supernaw' s BNA release, Red & Rio Grande, the sad ballad conjures images which are all too common in the fabric of American society today. Hats off to Super- naw for tackling such a serious subject. Richard Landis produced. TANYA TUCKER "Soon" (Liberty DPRO- 79830) The title cut from her new Liberty album, "Soon" is another good cheatin' song. Written by Casey Kelly & Bob Regan, the song is extremely well-crafted with Tanya wrapping those husky vocals around it and making it her own. An examination of a no-win affair, the sad ballad tells of heartache and pain while offer- ing probable solutions. Watch TNN & CMT for the accompanying video. Jerry Crutchfield produced. PICK OF THE WEEK ANDY CHILDS "Broken" (RCA 07883-88253-2/4) Smokin' rhythms, brilliant fiddle and carefully articulated phrasing push this one way over the top! It might just be the one Andy Childs needs to make his mark with radio. Written by Thom Schuyler, the upbeat ditty gives some insight into the reasons we fall in love even when we know we might get hurt. Good stuff! Radio's gonna love it. From his RCA debut, Andy Childs, Josh Leo & Mark Wright produced.

Martinez NERISSA: Nerissa (Active/Atlantic 4-92268). Producers: Various. Over much of this album, Nerissa's smoky vocals ride atop a cornucopia of dance beats and electronic wash. Nerissa doesn't try to re-invent the wheel on this debut collection, but she does find the right vocal niches on most tracks. Cuts like "The Cure," the groovy ballad "Stars" (complete with Marty Kirsch's tasty sax fills), a cover of the R&B classic 'In The Rain" (featuring rap by Ski), "Go On Get Out" and "Memories Of Love"clemonstrate that , 2this singer takes a few chances with the straight dance genre. H KASHAN: Love Is A Good Thang (Paragon/Solar72579-4). Producer: Kashan. Kashan has an engaging flair for mixing hip-hop ele- ments, rap and jazz in an unpretentitious sort of way. From the opening track, "Cool Summer Night," and its lilting groove, silky smooth female backing vocals and the mutecTtrumpet of Oscar Brashear, Kashan remains dis- arming. There are no real clunkers on this 10-track collec- tion. After the opening track, however, standouts include "Love Is a Gooa Thang" (the title track), "You Can Have It All" and "Check Me Out Cha'all." B DOMINO: Domino (Outburst OB 2461-2). Producers: AMG & Domino. There's some really compelling R&B music, thumping grooves and some sly lyrics thatKeep this album interest- ing. Domino prefers musical textures to minimalist at- titude, polyrhythmic counterpoint to monolithic groove, and some singing with his rap on this 10-track cutie. He's got a sense ofTiumor with the music (most evident on the tracks "A.F.D." and "Sweet Potatoe Pie"). But he also shows up funky and intense on tracks such as "Ghetto Jam," "Do You Qualify/” "Jam" and "Diggady Domino." SAMPLE THIS: Sample This (Elektra 9 61462-2). Producer: Anton Pukshansky . This is obviously a statement, an effort to make a case for live music that offers some sense of adventure. In a pop context. Sample This is adventurous. And Traedonya's throaty vocals will makeyou want to sample more of the music on this jazz/funk-influenced record. There are some Brand New Heavisms and retro-soul licks on this record (especially on the track "Shake That Egg"). This is part of the evolving jazz as contemporary pop movement that incorporates acid house ana other soul permuta- tions. PICK OF THE WEEK VINX: The Storyteller (Pangaea/1. R.S. 0777 7 13206 20). Producers: Greg Poree & Vinx. It's evident on this disc that Vinx has become comfortable with a personal vocal style. No longer does he sample the styles of forebearers such as Leon Thomas, A1 Jarreau or Bobby McFerrin. Vinx has affected a distinct frame for his unique vocalese. His warm, soothingvocal tone is evident throughout this 15-song third album by Vinx with producer Greg Poree. The only fragmentation—and this is not a drawback in this instance—is in the musical idioms Vinx has chosen to explore. He's at his pop jazz best on "Forever Yours"; he gets downright funky and danceable on "Living In The Metro"; and he gets intercontinentally ethnic on tracks like "Moondance" and "Amida."
